t: Great Partnerships Defer to Expertise and Passion
q: Making decisions together requires working through complex issues and different points of view.
The first rule is to defer to the judgment of the party with deepest expertise on the issue.
The second rule is to defer to the passion and strong sentiment of one of the parties.

If either party finds the outcome so reprehensible, uncomfortable, or distasteful, the parties then simply postpone or shelve the decision altogether to preserve the relationship and to offset future bitterness.
Good relationships deal with the potential potholes in the road long before they start driving.

t: Value Indicator: "When Am I Ever Going to Use This?"
q: This student's heart has been influenced at least a bit by the dominant utilitarian mentality that Westerners tend to bring to education: "If I can't see how what I'm learning is useful, then what I'm learning is a waste of time.
This student is genuinely struggling to WANT to do the work at hand. Something about it is repulsive to them — it is exerting a repulsive effect on their will.
As much as I wish student beliefs about my class were like little on/off switches, they act way more like different kinds of plants in a vibrant, interconnected garden ecosystem. They all connect.

These take time to improve — after all, as teachers we are in the counterculture business, and cultivating a counterculture isn't done in a day — but can slowly but steadily be helped through Mini-Sermons, Feasts of Knowledge, and Valued Within methods.
I wrote it because I wanted to address the common difficulties I encounter as a teacher, such as the difficulty I opened this article with.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Argues For A Misbehaving Friend
q: I recommend turning and walking away as soon as you deliver your consequence. Always. Never hang around and wait for an argument or response from the misbehaving student.
When you hear arguments and denials aimed at your back, you must ignore for now. Yes, it’s hard. You’d love to spin around and put the lying student in their place.
Once you’re calm and they’ve given up the charade, approach and deliver a consequence for calling out. Then turn and walk away the same as always.
Done just this way, it will leave them silent, humbled, and dissuaded from ever again dishonestly defending what is indefensible.
The most important lesson is to have a singular way of enforcing consequences that never changes and that enables you to follow through without fear, stress, or frustration.

t: Dont Tell People They Are Wrong - Tell Them How Right You Are Instead
q: The fact is, no one likes to be told they are wrong. Once told they are wrong, people stop listening and get defensive about their views.
The shock, dismay, or offense of being told they are wrong lasts beyond the initial negative reaction.
The better choice is to avoid ever labeling what others think or conclude as wrong, and instead simply emphasize how right you are.

Interesting suggestion, let me tell you what I believe…” or “I haven’t thought of that, but let me tell you what I have thought of…” are examples of not calling out what is wrong but instead moving quickly to what you believe is right.
The better habit is to give up telling others they don’t get it and to focus on what you believe is right.
Everyone is wrong now and again, but good leaders don’t rub it in.

t: Leading Team Members Who Dont Want a Relationship and Want to Be Left Alone to Do Their Work
q: In a challenge to the modern orthodoxy, some team members don’t want a relationship with their leader, preferring instead to do their work independently and remotely.
How does a leader engage team members who are good at what they do but disengage in an instant and have little desire to build a deeper connection to the leader, the organization, or its vision?
No team or organization can absorb beliefs and practices that are contrary to how it operates.
The best leaders ask team members to accommodate and adapt to the organization and not the other way around.
Those who insist on independence are welcome to take their skills elsewhere.

t: Where Do You Stand With Your Leader
q: Here are the questions and requests team members utilize with leaders ranked in a hierarchy of trust from low to high
It is not unusual for those with little experience, either with an assignment or the leader, to be required to operate at levels 1 or 2.
Leaders generally don’t let team members graduate from one level to the next.
If the trust level is lower than you want it to be, don’t ask for permission to move up the ladder.
Just engage at the next level and see how your leader responds. Take the chance. Trust is not only earned, it is also negotiated.

t: Next Year, Don't Start With Belonging
q: Belonging and community are critical to human flourishing — no doubt about it. But folks typically don't get much flourishing juice out of belonging to groups of people they really don't want to belong to.

You can play all the get-to-know-you games you want, do a thousand ice breakers, and use every team-building activity on the Internet, but unless your class has something that I believe is Valuable, unless you've made clear to me what kinds of Effort will help me grow…I'm still going to be watching the clock until I can leave.
This is why Belonging is at the top of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid. If you take care to do specific things that cultivate the four key beliefs below, Belonging is easy to put in place on top.
Once those beliefs are in place, now you can point out to the student that he's a reader, that she's a mathematician. Because now you've got PROOF.
See how small the Belonging section is? That's on purpose. Only one of the 10 strategies I unpack in the book focuses on Belonging.

t: Teaching Grit
q: Since the late 16th century, the word has been used to refer to a strength of human character, denoting pluckiness and tenacity.
Gritty people work strenuously toward challenges and maintain a constant effort despite setbacks and moments of failure.
The Hard Thing Rule is the daily practice of something outside your comfort zone.
They give up time, energy, and resources for the kind of practice that is uncomfortable and takes away from more pleasurable pursuits.
They promote the idea that the stubborn refusal to quit is a cardinal virtue.
The end result is a tad more Grit. Enduring the uncomfortable for a larger purpose is something people can learn if done in everyday practice.

t: The Secret of Olympic Motivation
q: Prior to his ultimate success on the water, two-time Olympic gold medalist rower Alex Gregory had the drive and skill to compete at the highest level for himself and Great Britain.
It was there Gregory learned the secret of Olympic motivation. But not on the water.
As Alex Gregory watched the family, he became overwhelmed by their emotion and affection for their son and brother.
He knew then that whatever it took, he wanted his family to feel those emotions and pride about him.
For Gregory, like so many other Olympians, the secret to motivation was to want his family to experience the thrill of victory with him.

t: Should YOU Write a Book About Teaching?
q: If writing a book about teaching is something you've thought about more than ten times, then let's start with: Yes — I think you should take the compulsion seriously.
But the thing to take away is that writing about teaching did something inside of them that not writing about teaching could not.

Writing confronts you with your lack of clarity. It's one thing to have amazing conversations about pedagogy with your hallway colleagues or folks at a conference. Conversations like these are critical to creating great books, but they aren't enough to produce good work.

Writing about teaching will make you feel like an imposter. When you're in the book-writing process, your heart becomes especially sensitive to the ways in which your teaching practice is lacking, especially in comparison to others.
Just because I'm an oddball who sometimes finds himself compelled to write books doesn't mean I'm of any greater value than the fearfully and wonderfully wrought colleague down the hall.

Writing a book is a horrible, exhausting struggle, like a long bout of some painful illness. One would never undertake such a thing if one were not driven on by some demon whom one can neither resist nor understand.

t: Learn to Treat Senior Leaders as a Resource and Not as an Authority
q: More seasoned, experienced, and senior leaders often get involved with matters across the organization.
The more powerful tact with senior leaders is to treat them as a resource and ask them to do things that help the situation and the team below them.
When explained with conviction and a detailed set of instructions, asking senior leaders to be a resource makes sense to them.
The key is to accomplish this frame and beat the senior leader to the starting line before a situation or project begins to unfold.
When asked to be a resource to the team and to play a specific role, senior leaders are typically delighted to comply.

t: How To Be A Great Teacher With No Personality https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2024/05/23/how-to-be-a-great-teacher-with-no-personality/
q: The first thing that jumped out at me, however, was that his students were happy. Lots of smiles, open body language, and an eagerness to learn.
It was not only clean and organized, with cabinets and drawers labeled and color-coded, but it was aesthetically pleasing.
He followed through calmly. His personality didn’t change whatsoever while going through the steps he had clearly modeled for his students.
He replaced performance with activities and projects students love. He got them moving and building and creating through his innovative ideas.
It showed me that when you seek perfection in just a small number of areas, the overall impact can be so great that it all but eliminates the need for teacher charisma and personality.

t: Whats in Your Way
q: Good leaders do everything in their power to remove obstacles that prevent team members from being the most productive they can be.
There may be structural issues inherent to the team or organization that get in the way.
Usually, one of the biggest impediments to productivity team members face is the leader.
Asking, “What do I do that makes your work more difficult than it should be?” or “What could I do to make your job or work much easier?” will also open up the conversation.
This question often jars a team member and gets them to honestly reflect on their role and accountability in addressing their own productivity.
Top performers never allow what they can’t do to thwart what they can do.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Laughs When You Give Another Student A Consequence
q: Laughter in this situation is infuriating because it makes light of the sacredness of uninterrupted learning. It also mocks the dignity of a classmate, borders on bullying.
Anticipate its possibility every time you give a consequence, especially at the beginning of the year when your students don’t know you or your staggeringly consistent follow through.
After you give a consequence in response to the initial disruption, pause. Wait a beat. Allow a moment of stillness and silence before returning to your lesson.
Hope isn’t a classroom management strategy. Nor is using your wits.
Effective classroom management is more science than art. Student behavior is predictable if you know the secrets, motivations, and leverages that drive it where you want it to go.

t: What a Suggestion Box Suggests About Your Team
q: Asking team members to offer ideas, suggestions, and complaints through an anonymous suggestion box has been a historically popular way for leaders to learn what others are really thinking.
The benefits of anonymous feedback and suggestions with large teams and groups are well-known.
But, by and large, suggestion boxes offer more advantages than disadvantages, and for large groups and teams, they are an invaluable source for innovative ideas and involvement.

When used by leaders in smaller teams and settings, suggestion boxes stifle open dialogue and create an expectation that people don’t feel safe unless they have an anonymous outlet to express their candid views.
Rather than fueling any unwillingness to share honestly in team discussions, good leaders reject forums for anonymous feedback and fix the real problem.
Building trust within a small team requires an expectation of peer-like dialogue without distinction of status, experience, or authority.

t: End of Year Efficacy Booster: Unpacking Outcomes via Conversation Challenge https://davestuartjr.com/end-of-year-efficacy-booster-unpacking-outcomes-via-conversation-challeng
q: This simple activity is a great example of Strategy 9 in The Will to Learn: Unpack Outcomes, Good or Bad. You're providing clear directions and a motivation context within which students can look at and think about the results of their efforts.
Whether their outcomes are good or bad, this kind of effort helps to cultivate a clearer sense for students of what success is and why it is or isn't happening for them.

Once you hit "go" on the timer, walk around and listen in. Coach where needed. Gather insights into where they are struggling and where they are succeeding. These 3-4 minutes are rich in formative information.

Give it a shot. The worst thing that can happen is that your students have some (brief) unproductive conversations. But even then, you can then unpack that bad outcome and grow clearer about how to get better outcomes next time.

Based on promising results at the end of the previous year, I went into this school year knowing I wanted to try making it my best pop-up debate year ever. Twenty PUDs later, I can say: mission accomplished.

t: Failure to Rescue
q: Failure to Rescue refers to a delay in recognizing and responding to a patient’s needs or complications, usually resulting in death.
What distinguishes good from great in a hospital setting is not about failing less, but in rescuing more.
In the words of one famous physician, “The harshest failure is the failure to rescue someone who needs you.
A Failure to Rescue or develop others’ talents is a problem that plagues too many leaders.
It speaks to the idea of building a “mastery of rescue,” as surgeon and author Atul Gawande likes to describe it.
How many average performers have you developed into top performers in your career?

t: #63 Challenge Students to Think of a Correct Answer That No-One Else Will Think Of
q: In my Tips for Teachers book, I describe three frameworks I use to enable students to generate their own examples, which gives me powerful insight into their understanding.
The bottom two boxes are designed to encourage students to generate boundary examples - in other words, examples right on the edge of what is and what is not true.
Boundary examples reveal the depth of a student’s understanding and can draw out key misconceptions.
The problem I found, however, was students did not know what the bottom-left box meant.
Once students have filled in all four boxes, I ask them to swap with their partner who then checks them.
We then discuss any examples labelled with a question mark as a class, as you can be sure these are the very examples right at the boundary of a concept and thus worthy of further investigation.

t: Do You Know Who I Am
q: By now, anyone with an internet connection knows that the top-ranked golfer in the world, Scottie Scheffler, was arrested while driving to the golf course at the PGA Championship in Kentucky.
Scheffler didn’t make it about himself, his status, or his fame.
Most impressively, he never uttered the words, “Do you know who I am?” Those are ugly words to anyone who understands leadership.
Taking situations more seriously than themselves is what good people and leaders do.
In Scheffler’s case, the only way to de-escalate the conflict was to make himself unimportant in the moment.
Taking oneself too seriously is a challenge many leaders face and fail.

t: The Right Practice Challenge Jump Starts Learning and Elevates Performance
q: Anytime we practice a task that is too difficult for us, learning and performance both suffer.
Interestingly, a task that is too easy compared to our skill level stunts learning and improvement, as well.
While repetition builds muscle and intellectual memory, it is raising the bar through challenge that most elevates performance.
The key is to design a challenge that pushes the limit of your current skills without causing so much frustration and anxiety as to undermine confidence.

Performers in any field get better by practicing difficult tasks. But only the right challenge at the right time allows performers to acquire and retain the important learning that improves long-term skill.

t: Independent Feedback Loops
q: Let's call scenario A an 'independent feedback loop'. This is where the user receives feedback which they can act upon instantly with no direct input from another expert needed.
For those who got some or most wrong, their time spent practising at best was a waste and at worst has helped embed some misconceptions which might move learning backwards for them.

If the problems require multiple steps to complete then, by using backwards faded examples which add an extra step as the questions develop, combined with answers being shared, leaners will be able to pinpoint the exact step at which they have a gap in their learning.
Giving learners explicit success criteria to hit at specific points can help them self-assess their work.
Let us not forget that there is also plenty that can be done, through careful thought and task design, to ensure that time spent practising is always time well spent.

t: Everything You Need to Know About Exam Stress
q: The nature of exam stress lies in its ability to trigger the body's 'fight or flight' response. This physiological reaction means a student will either be able to tackle the exam effectively or be unable to perform as they are overwhelmed with anxiety.
Research suggests that during examination periods, students not only experience increased levels of stress markers such as blood pressure, but also demonstrate a decrease in social contact.

A significant body of research links test anxiety with disrupted sleep patterns. For example, one study found that students with high levels of test anxiety reported poorer sleep quality, including difficulties falling asleep and staying asleep.
Students who take practice tests as part of their study regimen show improved memory and performance on actual exams.
Exams will always be synonymous with a certain degree of stress. And that can be a good thing. It can help people work harder and focus more. But too much stress can clearly hurt.

t: Developing a Strategic Knowledge for Long-Term Credibility
q: Team members have a deep respect for colleagues who project depth and expertise.
Such expertise is often called a “strategic knowledge” because of its ability to raise the standard of what it means to be an expert.
Developing a strategic knowledge is always intentional and requires a deep commitment to study and exploration, often over many years.
Because of this knowledge, they commonly draw analogies, metaphors, and examples from this domain to improve discussions and decisions on just about anything.
Examine the most credible leaders in any organization, and you will see they know more about one subject than just about anyone else.

q: I can say with absolute certainty that GPT-4o will only help certain learners this certain thoughts about certain kinds of math. This is true of every new tool or medium.
But calculation is to mathematics what chopping onions is to hosting a dinner party. It is important, but it is not central. It is not a prerequisite for other kinds of work.

t: Data Is Sometimes the Best Answer for Overcoming Resistance to Feedback
q: Data, when collected and presented well, is undeniable. It sets the record straight like nothing else can.
Think of it this way. When 12 people who know you well tell you that you walk and quack like a duck, you do.
To ensure the point is made, they will typically collect more data than they even need to.
Many will expect the data to confirm their views, not negate them.
Perception is a reality impossible to deny if it comes from many places.

t: Apologizing for Other Peoples Bad Behavior Underscores Your Values
q: When people observe others behaving poorly, rudely, or inappropriately, they typically shake their head and ignore the episode.
Apologizing to the recipient of this poor behavior by acknowledging the inappropriate actions and expressing regret that they had to endure it is what good leaders do.
It simply needs to express concern for the party on the receiving end and convey regret that the incident occurred.
Leaders who make a habit of apologizing for the bad behavior of others show themselves to stand for people and relationships.
They use an apology to those on the receiving end to send the most powerful message.
Some actions speak louder than others. Apologies speak volumes about a leader.

t: The Essential Ingredients of a Highly Engaging Team Offsite
q: Highly engaging offsites typically have four distinct ingredients and a commitment to a fast pace with varying energy throughout the day and evening.
Off-sites that don’t end with significant work products, like action plans or decisions, are often seen as less valuable and engaging.
Allowing a celebrity speaker to yak at the group for an hour seems like a bright idea but misses the point.
The right topics will be a tad uncomfortable for people, but good leaders know the value of addressing the elephant in the room.
Boondoggles in the sun, near the water, and in the mountains where not much gets done are certainly more fun, unless you want to make a true difference for the team.

t: Administrators, You've GOT to Help Us With This ONE Thing Next Year
q: Administrators, if you don't have a locked-in, 95%-consistent cell phone policy that lives and breathes and happens each day in your school, this summer your teachers and your students need you to lead the charge on a policy for making this happen.

As principal Ben Berger put it in our interview, leading the charge at his school on a solid, consistent, clear, and non-optional cell phone sleeve policy has been "the biggest bang for the buck educational move I've implemented.
This isn't an optional thing or something you leave up to professional discretion — this is like hand-washing for doctors.

Rinse and repeat these moves all year long, and you will find that a problem that used to riddle your school evaporates like a cold morning dew. There'll still be problems, but they won't be pervasive.
This type of leadership is NOT the job of your teachers, dear administrators — it is a part of your job as leaders. We need you to help us do "what's best for kids.
Unlike the latest buzzy trial headlines taking up our newsfeeds, the verdict has been in for a while on this matter of cell phones and secondary students.

t: Delivering a Tough Message About Their Flaws Starts With Your Flaws
q: Some team members don’t know themselves well and fight the same demons on many days.
But making deep character flaws explicit, no matter how good a leader’s intentions might be, will often produce resistance and rejection.
They start with themselves. They point out their flaws and areas for development.
Then they turn to the team member and ask, “What about you?
By starting with themselves and admitting their flaws with a genuine vulnerability, leaders level the playing field and wipe away the defensiveness that undermines a productive conversation.
As in so many difficult situations, it starts with the leader.

t: #62 Plan Your Follow-Up Question in Advance
q: A clear teacher explanation, followed by a re-check for understanding using a question that assesses the same skill, provides much more reliable evidence that our response has had the intended impact than the classic: Does that make sense?
One of the critical misconceptions students have about the laws of indices is knowing whether to add or multiply the powers. With a 2 and 2, you can do it either way and still be correct.
In the heat of a lesson, with many things vying for our limited attention, the chance of us making up as good a follow-up question as we would outside this environment is minimal.
In the coaching session afterwards, I asked him why he did a follow-up question for the fractions question but not one for the Venn Diagrams question.
Creating a follow-up question on the spot may be tempting. But for an extra couple of minutes of planning time, I recommend preparing it in advance.

t: The Pain of Discipline or the Pain of Regret
q: Author Jim Rohn suggests that all leaders suffer from one of two ailments: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret.
Author and former Navy Seal Jocko Willink suggests that discipline is freedom.
Very few leaders actually choose the path of self-satisfaction mindfully. Instead, they simply engage with less discipline than they should and therefore make the choice passively.
Discipline in one area, such as exercise or sleep, doesn’t always equate to self-regulation in other areas, such as saying no to unnecessary commitments.
The key to enhancing discipline is to engage in honest self-review.
The ability to do unpleasant things to build a foundation for success is what discipline is all about.

t: Is Email Feedback a Waste of Time?
q: Feedback is best when it is co-constructed between both parties, rather than simply transmitted by the observer.

Feedback sent via email doesn't really afford any of the above, and so is unlikely to be helpful. It probably won't lead to a teacher actually changing their practice. In fact, Tom describes this as outright rude.

So should we just ditch email feedback? I’m not sure. I think part of this comes down to playing the percentages game and considering a cost-benefit analysis – do I think this system is causing more harm than good?
It's not 'You did X, you should have done Y' rather it's 'I noticed X happened when you did Y. What might have happened if you'd tried Z instead?'
So thank you, Tom. This was useful feedback that I’m responding to. And, ironically, it was a blogpost that did this, something even less direct, personalised and co-constructed than an email!

t: Improving Independent Learning
q: A lack of independence is a commonplace issue in education, but less common is an agreed way forward to best address the issue of inadequate independent learning or ‘learned helplessness’.

Why do I particularly like this phrase? For one, it challenges the misconception about the innateness of effective independent learning. Even for the pupils who appear most helpless, a sustained approach to teaching strategies to develop independence is workable.
A list of strategy is no quick-fix to what are complex challenges of course. Many of these approaches have been shared with best intent, but little has changed.
Too often, pupils try them once, don't quite understand how to enact them well, so drop the strategy and carry on regardless.
'Naming', carefully 'framing', and planning for 'sustaining' the use of these independently learning strategies is a strong start.

t: Can Students Catch Attention? Introducing Attention Contagion tagion/
q: That is: if Student A pays attention, will that attentiveness cause Student B to pay more attention as well? Or, if Student A seems inattentive, what happens with Student B?
Well, when A paid attention, B reported focusing more, focused more, got less drowsy, and fidgeted less, took more notes, and remembered slightly more on a subsequent multiple-choice quiz.
Sure enough, Forrin's team found the same results. Student B caught Student A's inattention, even if s/he couldn't see it.
If attention contagion is a thing, I can help that-student-right-there pay attention by ensuring ALL students are paying attention.
I should point out that the concept of 'attention contagion' is quite new — and its newness means we don't have much research at all on the topic.

Here, Alex suggests some concrete strategies that can help. I really like the 'name it, then frame it' approach.
For what it’s worth, I am on Tom’s side of the debate here, but it is always worth being challenged by alternative perspectives.

t: Why You Should Limit Group Work
q: For students who are motivated and determined to do well, group work is an exercise in frustration and unfairness. They do all or most of the work.
They’re far more aware of the sham of group work than their teachers, who either have their heads in the sand or know better but choose not to do anything about it.

Individual skills in reading, writing, and math should far and away be the priority. Throwing students below grade level into time-eating groups where they contribute almost nothing makes little sense.
Give grades based on the individual work that is produced. Although counterintuitive, this tact produces far better and higher quality than giving every student the same group grade.
Great teachers and administrators are skeptical. They question and test everything to determine what really works.

t: The Teaching Power of a Double Demonstration
q: Leaders intuitively know that giving team members too much direction or process can stunt their development.
This is when leaders ask a team member to execute on a task or assignment without much direction and to keep their end product or solution to themselves for a time.
This Double Demonstration often turbo-charges learning in a way nothing else can.
It is not uncommon for a team member to finally understand what has been holding them back in creating better outcomes.
By definition, high performance is a demonstration of skill.
Exposing the assumptions, choices, and strategies of high performance is a lens into learning like none other.

t: How Self-Aware Are You
q: If there were only one quality from which to predict lifetime success, self-awareness would have to be on the shortlist.
They have an objective view of their strengths and their weaknesses.
Perhaps most importantly, they understand the contrast between how they see themselves and how others see them.
They judge their accuracy by observing how others respond to their choices in style, messages, actions, and decisions.
The best leaders agree with the ancient Greeks that knowing yourself is the beginning of wisdom.

t: End of Year Value Booster: the Led Tasso
q: On most days, you and I need to be the folks in the room who are rock solid in our grasp of why the work of learning in our class matters. If we don't know the Value of the work, we can't expect our students to.
Students, I've had it. I can no longer see why the work we do in here is worthwhile. In fact, I'm convinced it's not. It's garbage. It's pointless. It's done nothing for you.

I mean, think about it: when are you ever going to need to read literature in real life? To write essays? To take notes on new material? To engage in pop-up debates? These are not real-world activities — they are contrived, cutesy school things.

This is great for the end of the school year because it gives your students practice at what they'll need to do for the rest of their lives: figure out why the work of learning is valuable, even when that Value has its skeptics, even when the person in charge has lost their way.
Group your students into fours and give the groups three minutes to come up with the best arguments they can muster. At the end of the time, each group nominates a speaker to make their best case.

t: #61 Sometimes Mini-Whiteboards Are Not the Best Way to Collect Whole-Class Data

Notice how difficult it is to identify students’ choices of answers, especially those at the back.
My preferred way of collecting data for multiple-choice diagnosis questions is to use coloured ABCD cards or head down first on head.
With 30 students in the class, there was too much data to identify who was correct and who was not.
This was difficult to see, compounded by dirty boards and small writing.

In each of the examples above, whiteboards could be used for students to do their working out on, but then another tool could have been used to make the required quick-fire analysis of the data more manageable.

t: Everything You Own Owns a Piece of You, Too
q: As they accumulate more material possessions, people typically come to a realization that perhaps should have been clear much earlier.
We don’t own anything of true value that doesn’t require our time, attention, maintenance, and resources.
When we agree to the responsibilities and commitments required in an elevated position, we invariably “own” the role as if it were a tangible thing.
It takes an enormous amount of time, energy, and creativity to excel at leading others.
Metaphorically speaking, we pay rent in time and worry for the most valuable things we own.

t: Its Time to Discard the Sandwich Technique for Giving Feedback
q: In many organizations, the technique is known as a Crap Sandwich because everyone knows that the center of the sandwich tastes like rubbish.
After a few experiences with this technique, those on the receiving end often feel manipulated by it.
The key is to make this positive statement as detailed and vivid as the criticism will likely be.
The more specific, thorough, and elaborate the positive statement, the more likely it is to be seen as sincere and genuine.
Going straight to the criticism or attempting to offset it with an artificial affirmation creates heavy resistance and encourages people to reject what they are hearing.
Kill the sandwich technique and replace it with feedback that operates in balance.

t: A Proposal for Saving Five Million Hours per Year (One Day per Teacher) of Workload, Without Harming Pupil Achievement per-teacher-of-workload-without-harming-pupil-achievement/
q: Most pupils move very little. On a scale where two thirds of pupils score between 85 and 115, half of pupils’ Spring term scores are within 5 points of their Autumn term score.
When we look at the change across one term (the top two graphs), only about one in twenty (5-7%) see a fall in test scores that can be detected with a well-designed test.

We have not encountered any examples of schools where the actions arising after a half termly deposit of attainment data justify the time investment required by teachers to facilitate six data collection points a year.
But when it comes to capturing pupil-level change from one term to the next, termly testing is only informative for a very small minority of pupils.
Across all three groups, this amounts to a saving of 4.95m hours of workload per year, which is just over one day per year (8.7 hours) for every teacher in the country.

t: 3-Read Friday #35: Workload, Prior Knowledge, and Mini Whiteboard Pitfalls
q: If your Senior Leadership Team has not read Sam’s latest post, print a copy and anonymously drop it on their desk.
It is a rallying cry against the common practice of regular student testing which aims to track pupil progress and then target interventions.
Like Adam, I regularly watch lessons where relevant prior knowledge is mentioned but not explicitly assessed.
Adam suggests four reasons why this happens and suggests strategies for ensuring the assessment of prior knowledge plays a central role in our lessons.
But I had to include this post as it discusses some potential drawbacks of overusing mini-whiteboards.
And that is something that a mini-whiteboard evangelist like myself needs to read once in a while.

t: How To Handle Students Who Do Nothing
q: So you rush over and ask what the problem is. You prod and push. You flatter and threaten. You counsel and kneel down to reteach.
Although counterintuitive—and blasphemy in the current educational milieu—the best thing you can do for them is let them be.
Simply allow the weight of not doing the assignment (i.e. its effect on grades, academic performance, skill acquisition, loss of recess, etc.) shift from burdening you to them.
For students unaccustomed to being left without the world rushing to lighten their accountability, it takes a while for the lesson to sink in. But sink in it will.
It puts them into a highly pleasurable flow state, where time distorts and contentment soothes. It raises their self-worth and provides a sense of real accomplishment.

t: Selecting Value-Congruent Vendors, Suppliers, and Partners
q: Because these vendors, suppliers, and partners reflect both the brand and quality of the enterprise, their selection is of the utmost importance for long-term success.
This mismatch erodes the quality of the organization with every contract, new or renewed, that is selected primarily on cost.
Some will routinely reduce the quality of their work just to compete on price.
Price is of little consequence if the services, products, or advice offered are inconsistent with what the enterprise stands for and hopes to instill in others.
Remember this: the cost of success is far cheaper than the price of misalignment and failure.
